B1_extra.label: Interleaved practice vs. blocked practice — math test scores 30 days later
B1_extra.unit: percent correct on delayed test (interleaved) vs 42 percent (blocked), Cohen's d = 0.79
B1_extra.what_it_means: 126 seventh-graders practiced the same math problems over 3 months, either interleaved (mixed problem types within an assignment) or in the usual blocked-by-type order. On an unannounced test given 30 days after the final review, students scored 74% on material they had practiced in interleaved order vs. 42% on material practiced in blocked order — a large effect (d = 0.79).

source.title: Interleaved practice improves mathematics learning.
source.verbatim: Students tested 30 days after the review showed a large benefit of interleaving, 74% (SD = 39%) vs. 42% (SD = 43%), t(62) = 4.54, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.79, 95% confidence interval (CI) [0.43, 1.15].

B1_extra.label: Self-explanation prompts vs. no self-explanation — meta-analytic effect on learning
B1_extra.what_it_means: Across 69 effect sizes pooled from 64 separate research reports, prompting learners to explain material to themselves while studying or solving problems (vs. not prompting them to) produced a medium-sized, statistically reliable improvement in learning outcomes (g = .55).

source.title: Inducing Self-Explanation: a Meta-Analysis
source.verbatim: Our systematic search of relevant bibliographic databases identified 69 effect sizes (from 64 research reports) which met certain inclusion criteria. The overall weighted mean effect size using a random effects model was g = .55. ... an overall point estimate of g = .55 with a 95% confidence interval ranging from .45 to .65

B3_extra.label: Brief mental 'breaks' (task-switch) prevent the vigilance decrement
B3_extra.unit: F(3,240), ANOVA effect of block on vigilance sensitivity (A'); not significant for the brief-break group vs F(3,240) > 4.62, p < .005 for the three continuous-work groups
B3_extra.what_it_means: In a 40-minute continuous attention task, people who were briefly interrupted 3 times to recall a memorized set of digits (a 'switch'/break) showed NO decline in vigilance performance across the task [F(3,240)=0.89, not significant]. In contrast, three other groups who worked continuously without that kind of break (including a group carrying the same memory load without ever being interrupted to use it) all showed a significant decline in performance over blocks [F(3,240) > 4.62, p < .005 in each case].

source.title: Brief and rare mental “breaks” keep you focused: Deactivation and reactivation of task goals preempt vigilance decrements
source.verbatim: Simple main effects of Block were significant for Control, No-switch, and Digit-ignored conditions [Fs(3, 240) > 4.62, p < .005]. Post-hoc tests (Ryan, 1960) indicated that in the Control and Digit-ignored conditions, sensitivity significantly declined over the 3rd and 4th blocks; and that in the No-switch condition sensitivity declined on the 4th block (p < .05). Most crucially, sensitivity in the Switch condition did not decrease as a function of experimental block [F(3, 240) = 0.89, ns.].

B3_extra.label: Writing a specific to-do list at bedtime speeds sleep onset
B3_extra.what_it_means: In a sleep-lab study using overnight polysomnography (not self-report), 57 healthy young adults spent 5 minutes before lights-out either writing a to-do list of upcoming tasks or journaling about tasks they'd already completed. The to-do-list group fell asleep significantly faster than the completed-list group (d = 0.63), and the more specific their list, the faster they fell asleep.

source.title: The effects of bedtime writing on difficulty falling asleep: A polysomnographic study comparing to-do lists and completed activity lists.
source.verbatim: Participants who wrote a To-Do List fell asleep significantly more quickly than those who wrote a Completed List, t(55) = 2.32, p = 0.02, d = .63.

B2_extra.label: Spaced (gapped) restudy vs. same-day restudy — final recall
B2_extra.unit: percent increase in final recall for the optimal study gap vs. a zero-day (same-day) gap, Cohen's d = 1.1
B2_extra.what_it_means: Over 1,350 people learned a set of trivia facts, then reviewed them again after a gap ranging from 0 days to several months, then took a final test after a further delay of up to a year. Compared to reviewing the material the same day it was first learned (zero-day gap), waiting an optimal number of days before reviewing produced 64% more items recalled on the final test (d = 1.1) — this is an original experiment, not the earlier Cepeda 2006 meta-analysis.

source.title: Spacing Effects in Learning: A Temporal Ridgeline of Optimal Retention
source.verbatim: The effects of gap were very large in magnitude: For a fixed amount of study time, the optimal gap provided a 64% increase, d = 1.1, in final recall, and a 26% increase, d = 1.5, in final recognition, as compared to a zero-day gap (in the present article, d values refer to the comparison of zero-day versus optimal gap).

corrections.finding: The number IS genuinely in the primary source, just past where Round 1's verbatim quote stopped. Full sentence, from the paper's Results section (and repeated in the Figure 1 caption): "Collapsed across question type (verbatim and inference), the advantage of retrieval practice (M = 0.67) over elaborative studying with concept mapping (M = 0.45) represented about a 50% improvement in long-term retention scores [d = 1.50, F(1,38) = 21.63, ηp² = 0.36]." Figure 1 caption independently repeats it: "retrieval practice enhanced long-term learning above and beyond elaborative study with concept mapping by one and a half standard deviations (d = 1.50)..." So d=1.50 is correct and appears twice in the paper — Round 1's number was NOT fabricated or drifted from elsewhere, it was just quoted with an incomplete verbatim excerpt. Recommend: in method_claims_b1b2.json, extend that claim's verbatim string to include the full sentence through '[d = 1.50, F1,38 = 21.63, ηp² = 0.36].' so the value is self-contained in its own quote.
